itineraries.title: Romania: Oltenia, the Danube and the Iron Gates in 7 days
itineraries.subtitle: Follow the Danube and the Carpathian foothills, from Brâncovenesc monasteries to the Iron Gates gorges.
itineraries.notes: An itinerary weaving between monasteries and ancient sites along the Carpathian foothills and the Danube, ideal in spring and early autumn. Cruises through the Cazanele Dunării depend on river levels and weather: confirm departures from Orșova the day before.
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C, ideal for mountain roads and Danube gorges. Avoid July-August: scorching heat in the valley (35-40°C), exposed routes. Winter is cold and grey, snow possible at higher elevations.

visits.text: Outsized and chilling, the Palace of the Parliament remains one of the world's largest administrative buildings. Built under Ceaușescu's dictatorship, it now houses the chambers of Parliament and can only be visited with a guide; you'll see just a tiny fraction, but the halls take your breath away. Book Tuesday through Thursday between 9 and 11 am: tour buses arrive mid-morning and on weekends.

Founded by merchants from Leipzig in the fifteenth century, Lipscani Street forms the heart of the Centru Vechi, Bucharest's Old Town. Cobbled lanes, restored façades, terraces and cafés line up at the foot of old merchant houses. Make a detour to the Cărturești Carusel bookshop, housed in a white building with balustrades: one of the city's most beautiful.

Incense, carved columns and a silent courtyard: Stavropoleos Church surprises you in the lively heart of Lipscani. This little eighteenth-century Orthodox church conceals an inner courtyard and lapidarium away from the noise. Enter quietly, services may be underway; a few minutes are enough to catch your breath before heading back to the terraces.

activities.text: Book a table at Caru' cu bere, a brewery opened in 1899 with neo-Gothic woodwork and period stained glass. You'll eat hearty Romanian cuisine, sometimes with folk dancing in the evening, in décor that's worth the trip alone. The place is very popular: book online, especially on weekends.

practical_info.tip: Book online a few days ahead, evenings are often fully booked.

visits.text: City of tulips by day, dark memory below ground: the Pitești Prison Memorial recounts one of the harshest episodes of Communist Romania. The former prison, active from 1941 to 1977, was the scene of a re-education program through violence aimed at political prisoners. The visit is heavy but illuminating; plan on a guide for context, and skip this stop if you're traveling with young children.

The Argeș County Museum occupies the former neoclassical prefecture in the city center. Its sections trace the history, ethnography and natural sciences of the Argeș region, a good introduction before the monasteries. Allow an hour; check opening times online, they vary by season.

activities.text: Stroll through Trivale forest park, a vast green lung edging the city to the west. Shaded paths, ponds and fresh air: it's the ideal place to decompress after the prison memorial. If you pass in spring, the city is covered in tulips, its emblematic flower.

practical_info.tip: In spring, the tulip festival (Simfonia Lalelelor) brings the downtown parks to life.

visits.text: Hard to get more photogenic: Curtea de Argeș Monastery and its two twisted towers look like something from a fairy tale. Founded around 1512 by voivode Neagoe Basarab, the current building was rebuilt between 1875 and 1885 by French architect Lecomte du Noüy, who gave it its gilded decorations. It houses the necropolis of Romania's first kings. Arrive early, tour buses are already parking by mid-morning.

Legend has it that master mason Manole walled his wife alive within the walls so the church of Curtea de Argeș would stop collapsing every night. Manole's Fountain, opposite the monastery, is linked to this founding ballad of Romanian folklore. The fountain has nothing spectacular about it: it's the legend that merits the stop, read it before you go.

Founded in the fourteenth century, the Princely Court (Curtea Domnească) was the residence of the first princes of Wallachia, hence the city's name. Today partly ruined, it preserves within its walls Saint Nicholas Church, the oldest in the city, with medieval frescoes. The entrance is modest; the visit wraps up in half an hour.

Cozia Monastery, nestled on the banks of the Olt, was founded in 1388 by Mircea the Elder, who rests there. It's one of the finest examples of Byzantine-influenced Romanian medieval art, with ancient frescoes and white walls pressed against the valley. The view from the riverbank, of the buildings tight against the rock, is worth the stop alone. Pass before 10 am to enjoy the calm.

Cross the footbridge to Ostrov Monastery, built in 1522 on an island in the middle of the Olt (ostrov means "river island"). It preserves eighteenth-century paintings and a very peaceful flowered park, two steps from the center of Călimănești. It's a short, serene stop; entry is free.

The most accomplished of the Brâncovenesc monasteries is Hurezi, founded in 1690 by Prince Constantin Brâncoveanu and inscribed on UNESCO's list in 1993. Galleries with carved pillars, brightly colored frescoes, a painted refectory: the ensemble embodies this sober yet sumptuous style. It sits about 5 km from the village, surrounded by forest. Avoid holiday weekends, which are very busy.

activities.text: Step through the door of a Horezu pottery workshop, whose craftsmanship has been listed as UNESCO intangible heritage since 2012. The "Hurez rooster" adorns most pieces, shaped and painted by hand using gestures passed down through generations. If you visit in early June, the "Cocoșul de Hurez" fair brings together potters from across the country.

practical_info.tip: Buy directly from the workshop: fairer prices and much wider selection than in shops.

visits.text: Attested from the early sixteenth century, Polovragi Monastery guards the entrance to the Olteț gorges. Dedicated to the Dormition of the Mother of God, it's a quiet, flowered Byzantine ensemble with a beautiful portal and tree-lined avenue. Sunday market brings the village to life; take advantage and pass by late morning.

Local legends make Polovragi Cave (Peștera Polovragi) the dwelling of Zalmoxis, the god of the Getae-Dacians. The guided visit lasts about thirty minutes and passes through a gallery of stalactites, a few hundred meters from the monastery. Allow around €4 for entry; bring a jacket, the air is cool and damp.

activities.text: Walk behind the monastery to reach the Olteț Gorges (Cheile Oltețului), a narrow limestone canyon where the road squeezes between cliffs. Some trails branch off from there toward Buila-Vânturarița National Park. Good shoes recommended, the rock can be slippery after rain.

practical_info.tip: Park at the monastery and continue on foot, the canyon is tight for cars.

map_keywords: Gate of the Kiss Târgu Jiu

visits.text: Brâncuși's most famous work comes down to one word: the Endless Column, a metal shaft about 30 m tall erected in Column Park. Completed in 1937–1938 in homage to Romanian soldiers of the First World War, it stacks diamond-shaped modules toward the sky. The Târgu Jiu ensemble was inscribed on UNESCO's list in 2024. Come late in the day, the raking light sublimes the metal.

The Gate of the Kiss and the Table of Silence open the axis of the Calea Eroilor, in Constantin Brâncuși Park. The gate, five meters tall, reprises the kiss motif the sculptor worked on for thirty years; the round table is surrounded by twelve hourglass-shaped seats. Everything is freely accessible outdoors.

activities.text: Walk the Calea Eroilor, the roughly 1.3 km axis linking the Table of Silence to the Endless Column by way of the Gate of the Kiss and the Church of the Holy Apostles. It's a slow walk, designed as an initiatory path between two parks. Allow a good half hour of walking, plus time for pauses in front of each work.

practical_info.tip: Walk the axis in the direction table → column, as Brâncuși conceived it.

visits.text: Tismana Monastery, the oldest in Wallachia, was consecrated on August 15, 1377 by Saint Nicodim the Pious. Nestled among yew trees (tisă, which give it its name) at the bottom of a green valley, it combines Athonite and Romanian influences. August 15 remains a major pilgrimage day: expect crowds on that date.

activities.text: If water levels permit, climb up to Tismana Cave and waterfall that spurts above the monastery, about forty meters of elevation. The short trail skirts the forest and offers beautiful views of the white buildings. Slippery after rain: closed shoes recommended.

practical_info.tip: The waterfall's flow drops significantly in midsummer, more impressive in spring.

visits.text: Completed around 105 AD by Apollodorus of Damascus, Trajan's Bridge remained the world's longest bridge for over a thousand years, with its 1,135 m spanning the Danube. It served the Roman legions during the Dacian Wars, then was abandoned after the loss of Dacia. Only a few piers remain on the Romanian side, near the museum: a modest vestige, but charged with history.

The Iron Gates Region Museum sits beside the Roman ruins and brings together three sections: history of ancient Drobeta, ethnography of Mehedinți, and natural sciences dedicated to Danube fauna. A statue of Apollodorus of Damascus stands at the entrance. Open Tuesday to Sunday 9 am to 5 pm, entry around €5.50.

Raw concrete over 441 m in length: the Iron Gates Dam, at Gura Văii (15 km west), has blocked the Danube since the 1960s. It's a hydroelectric power station, a lock system and a bridge to Serbia all at once; its construction swallowed villages and roads. A small museum recounts this titanic project.

A city entirely rebuilt after the old town was submerged beneath the dam lake, Orșova is now the embarkation port for the Cazanele Dunării. Its flat waterfront, opening onto the river and the Serbian hills opposite, has nothing ancient but offers a beautiful expanse. It's mainly a practical base before the cruise: few visits in the town itself.

activities.text: Board early in the morning from Orșova: the first departure around 9 am offers the best light and fewer people on the Danube. The boats head upstream toward the Iron Gates gorges, passing Trajan's Tablet on the Serbian side and the Veterani Cave. Book the day before, especially in high season; departures depend on river level.

practical_info.tip: Check the weather: in strong winds, trips can be cancelled.

visits.text: A Romanian Mount Rushmore, cruder: the Rock Sculpture of Decebalus, Europe's tallest rock sculpture, fixes the last king of the Dacians into the cliff above the Danube. Carved from 1994 to 2004 by twelve sculptors, financed by entrepreneur Iosif Constantin Drăgan, it bears the Latin inscription "DECEBALUS REX - DRAGAN FECIT". You can see it from the road, but the best view is from the water.

activities.text: Glide by boat into the Cazanele Dunării, where the Danube squeezes between limestone cliffs rising several hundred meters. It's the most spectacular passage of the Iron Gates, on the border with Serbia, right below Decebalus's face. Trips depart mainly from Orșova and Eșelnița; morning recommended for light and calm.

practical_info.tip: Combine the trip with the Veterani Cave and Trajan's Tablet, visible from the boat.

visits.text: Rebuilt in 1645 by Matei Basarab, Mănăstirea Strehaia rises on an old court of the Craiovești boyars, attested from the fourteenth century. Constantin Brâncoveanu added a portico in 1693, and the church preserves a curious south-facing altar. It's an ideal stop to break up the Drobeta-Craiova road, on the DN6; allow about twenty minutes.

activities.text: Make a circuit of Strehaia's fortified remains: of five original towers, only the gate tower survives, near the vaulted cellars of the old princely palace and the enclosure wall. The ensemble, a classified historical monument, gives the monastery its air of a little fortress. Take the opportunity to stretch your legs before getting back behind the wheel.

practical_info.tip: The site is in the center of Strehaia, easy to access and free.

visits.text: The Jean Mihail Palace houses the Craiova Art Museum and eight works by Constantin Brâncuși, in rooms adorned with Carrara marble, Lyon silks and Murano crystal. Built between 1898 and 1907 by French architect Paul Gottereau, the building is a décor in itself. In 2026, the city celebrates the 150th anniversary of Brâncuși's birth.

The oldest civic building in the city, Casa Băniei (fifteenth century) recalls the medieval roots of Craiova, historic capital of Oltenia. It now houses an ethnographic section on the trades and customs of the region. It's two steps from the center, easy to link with the Art Museum on foot.

activities.text: Stroll through Nicolae Romanescu Park, designed by Frenchman Édouard Redont and awarded a gold medal at the 1900 Paris Universal Exposition. Winding paths, boating lake, suspension bridge and romantic folly: it's one of the country's largest urban parks. Allow an hour's walk to end your trip gently.

practical_info.tip: The park is a bit out of the way: allow 15 min by car from downtown.

visits.text: Cradle of the Brâncoveanu family, Brâncoveni Monastery blends two major building campaigns: that of Matei Basarab (1634–1640), who gave it enclosure walls and a bell tower, and that of Constantin Brâncoveanu, who erected the great church in 1699. The princely chambers now house a small museum. It's a logical final stop before shooting toward Bucharest, 20 km southwest of Slatina.

activities.text: Stop at the Izvorul Tămăduirii, the spring in the enclosure where, tradition says, Matei Basarab was cured of a skin disease gnawing at him. The avenue runs from the great carved wooden gate to the fortified courtyard and the little bolniță church. A few minutes suffice; entry is free, proper dress required.

practical_info.tip: The access road from the wooden gate was recently paved, arrival is easy.

seo.h1_title: Romania: Oltenia, the Danube and the Iron Gates in 7 days
seo.intro_paragraph: This 7 days road trip connects Bucharest to Craiova following the Carpathian foothills then the Danube. On the program: UNESCO-listed Brâncovenesc monasteries, Brâncuși sculptures in Târgu Jiu, Roman vestiges and the Iron Gates gorges. A less-traveled Romania, between Orthodox spirituality and river landscapes.
seo.seo_hook: UNESCO Hurezi Monastery, Brâncuși sculptures in Târgu Jiu and Decebalus statue on the Danube: 7 days in Oltenia and the Iron Gates.
